# Data Leakage in Simple HTTP Applications

This example examines a catalogue endpoint that accepts an item identifier in
`/catalogue/item/{id}`. That path segment is untrusted, attacker-controlled
input. The vulnerable baseline exposes sequential database IDs, making it cheap
to enumerate catalogue records and learn which resources exist.

The safer variant exposes a UUID instead. A UUID makes identifier guessing
impractical and reduces accidental disclosure through copied URLs, logs, and
browser history. It is not authorization: this deliberately small application
has no authenticated caller or ownership rule, so a UUID must not be treated as
permission to access a resource. The local H2 database and its sample data are
workshop fixtures, not a production-ready security design.

For resources that are not public, opaque identifiers are only defence in depth.
See the
[Broken Object-Level Authorization](../broken-object-level-authorization/)
example for authenticated, ownership-aware access checks.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- identify a URL path identifier as an untrusted input and potential
  data-disclosure point;
- demonstrate enumeration of resources that use predictable numeric identifiers;
- verify that the UUID variant rejects numeric identifiers and serves an item by
  its opaque identifier; and
- explain why opaque identifiers reduce enumeration but do not replace
  object-level authorization.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25 or newer](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- `curl` available on your PATH to send requests to the local service.

- `jq` available on your PATH to format JSON responses.

- `rsync` available on your PATH to copy the workshop fixture into the local
  source tree.

The Maven Wrapper downloads required Maven components and dependencies if they
are not already cached, so an initial build may require network access.

## The program to inspect

The baseline controller binds the attacker-controlled path segment to a `Long`
and looks up the entity by its sequential database primary key. It has no caller
identity or authorization check; whether catalogue data may be public is
therefore a product and security-policy decision outside this demonstration.

```java
package demo.catalogue;

import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

import static java.util.Objects.requireNonNull;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/catalogue/item")
public final class CatalogueItemController {

    private final CatalogueItemService service;

    public CatalogueItemController(final CatalogueItemService service) {
        this.service = requireNonNull(service, "Service cannot be null");
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<CatalogueItemTo> get(@PathVariable(value = "id") final Long id) {
        return service.findById(id)
                .map(CatalogueItemTo::of)
                .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
                .orElseGet(() -> ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
}
```

The fixture changes the public lookup key to a UUID. Its migration creates a
unique UUID for every existing item, and its controller binds that UUID before
looking it up. This is a visible contrast with the vulnerable baseline, but it
does not add authentication, tenant scoping, or ownership checks.

```java
package demo.catalogue;

import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

import java.util.UUID;

import static java.util.Objects.requireNonNull;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/catalogue/item")
public final class CatalogueItemController {

    private final CatalogueItemService service;

    public CatalogueItemController(final CatalogueItemService service) {
        this.service = requireNonNull(service, "Service cannot be null");
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<CatalogueItemTo> get(@PathVariable(value = "id") final UUID id) {
        return service.findByGuid(id)
                .map(CatalogueItemTo::of)
                .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
                .orElseGet(() -> ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
}
```

The fixture regression tests make the expected URL behaviour executable: a known
UUID returns the item, an unknown UUID returns `404`, and a numeric value is
rejected as malformed. They do not prove that a caller is authorized.

```java
package demo.catalogue;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure.AutoConfigureMockMvc;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.MockMvc;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.request.MockMvcRequestBuilders.get;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.jsonPath;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.status;

@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
class CatalogueItemControllerTest {

    @Autowired
    private MockMvc mockMvc;

    @Test
    void returnTheItemByGuidId() throws Exception {
        mockMvc.perform(get("/catalogue/item/81994f73-50c3-4035-b4e3-e81c5c250ddd"))
                .andExpect(status().isOk())
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.id").doesNotExist())
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.guid").value("81994f73-50c3-4035-b4e3-e81c5c250ddd"))
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.caption").value("Leather Sofa"))
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.description").value("A very nice and comfortable sofa"));
    }

    @Test
    void returnNotFoundWhenItemWithGivenGuidDoesNotExist() throws Exception {
        mockMvc.perform(get("/catalogue/item/17c15427-96a6-4457-8541-5346d53d4d9d"))
                .andExpect(status().isNotFound());
    }

    @Test
    void returnBadRequestWhenGivenNonUuid() throws Exception {
        mockMvc.perform(get("/catalogue/item/1"))
                .andExpect(status().isBadRequest());
    }
}
```

## Guided walkthrough

Run these commands from this example directory. They use only an in-memory
database and do not alter system configuration. The fixture-copy steps modify
the local `src` tree for the exercise; their cleanup restores the checked-in
vulnerable baseline.

1. Build and test the baseline. This establishes that the numeric-ID version
   starts from a working state; it is not evidence that the endpoint is safe.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the application was created.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -L 1 --prune './target'
   ```

   The packaged Spring Boot JAR and the original thin JAR.

   ```
   ./target
   ├── url-data-leak-1.0.0.jar
   └── url-data-leak-1.0.0.jar.original

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

2. Start the local baseline and wait, with a bounded retry, for it to accept
   requests. The PID file is used only to stop this workshop process.

   ```shell
   java -jar 'target/url-data-leak-1.0.0.jar' > 'target/application.log' 2>&1 &
   echo $! > 'target/application.pid'

   # Wait for the application to start
   until curl --silent --fail 'http://localhost:8080/catalogue/item/1' >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
   ```

3. Request item with id `1`.

   ```shell
   curl --silent --fail 'http://localhost:8080/catalogue/item/1' | jq
   ```

   The catalogue item with id `1`

   ```json
   {
     "id": 1,
     "caption": "Leather Sofa",
     "description": "A very nice and comfortable sofa"
   }
   ```

   Replace the identifier with `2`.

   ```shell
   curl --silent --fail 'http://localhost:8080/catalogue/item/2' | jq
   ```

   The catalogue item with id `2`

   ```json
   {
     "id": 2,
     "caption": "Wooden Table",
     "description": "A large table ideal for 6 to 8 people"
   }
   ```

   The two successful responses demonstrate that an observer can infer a
   predictable identifier scheme and enumerate records. The response data is
   only workshop sample data.

4. Stop the baseline before replacing its source files. This keeps the test and
   fixture transition deterministic.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat target/application.pid)" 2>/dev/null || true
   rm -f 'target/application.pid'
   ```

5. Reproduce the issue with a test first.

   Start by expressing the required behaviour as a regression test. Once the
   UUID URL contract is implemented, this test protects against accidentally
   reintroducing the numeric public identifier.

   The `fixtures` directory contains an updated `CatalogueItemControllerTest`
   class. Copy the fixture tests and run the build. The test suite should fail
   because the baseline accepts a numeric identifier and has no UUID lookup.

   This failure demonstrates that the required URL contract is absent. It does
   not demonstrate broken object-level authorization, because this application
   has no authenticated caller or authorization rule.

   ```shell
   rsync --archive 'fixtures/src/test' 'src'
   ```

   Run the tests. The new test should fail.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   The UUID URL-contract tests fail against the numeric-ID baseline.

   ```
   ...
   [ERROR] Failures:
   [ERROR]   CatalogueItemControllerTest.returnBadRequestWhenGivenNonUuid:38 Status expected:<400> but was:<200>
   [ERROR]   CatalogueItemControllerTest.returnNotFoundWhenItemWithGivenGuidDoesNotExist:32 Status expected:<404> but was:<400>
   [ERROR]   CatalogueItemControllerTest.returnTheItemByGuidId:22 Status expected:<200> but was:<400>
   [INFO]
   [ERROR] Tests run: 3, Failures: 3, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
   [INFO]
   [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
   [INFO] BUILD FAILURE
   [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
   ...
   ```

6. Fix the issue.

   This change needs more than replacing one field. First, add a unique,
   non-guessable UUID to the database and populate it for existing records.
   Update the application to look up items through that UUID while retaining
   the numeric ID internally for persistence and database relationships.

   In a production API, introduce and document the UUID-based endpoint before
   deprecating the numeric-ID endpoint. After every client has migrated and the
   deprecation period has ended, remove the predictable public path. This is a
   breaking API change and needs a managed rollout. For brevity, this example
   reuses `/catalogue/item/{id}`; the path segment changes from a numeric ID to
   a UUID.

   Copy the completed UUID variant, including its database migration, then
   rebuild. All tests should pass. The variant makes identifiers difficult to
   guess; it does not decide who may read an item.

   ```shell
   rsync --archive 'fixtures/src/main' 'src'
   ```

   Run the tests. All tests should now pass.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   The UUID URL-contract tests pass after the fixture is applied.

   ```
   ...
   [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
   [INFO] BUILD SUCCESS
   [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
   ...
   ```

   The application now expects a UUID and not an integer.

7. Start the UUID variant and wait for the known UUID to become available.

   ```shell
   java -jar 'target/url-data-leak-1.0.0.jar' > 'target/application.log' 2>&1 &
   echo $! > 'target/application.pid'

   until curl --silent --fail 'http://localhost:8080/catalogue/item/81994f73-50c3-4035-b4e3-e81c5c250ddd' >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
   ```

8. Request the item through its UUID. A copied URL can still disclose the UUID,
   so treat it as an identifier rather than a secret or an access token.

   ```shell
   curl --silent --fail 'http://localhost:8080/catalogue/item/81994f73-50c3-4035-b4e3-e81c5c250ddd' | jq
   ```

   The catalogue item with id `1`

   ```json
   {
     "guid": "81994f73-50c3-4035-b4e3-e81c5c250ddd",
     "caption": "Leather Sofa",
     "description": "A very nice and comfortable sofa"
   }
   ```

   Notice that the response no longer exposes the numeric `id`; it exposes the
   UUID instead. A correctly generated UUIDv4 has 2^122 possible random values
   (about 5.3 × 10^36), making blind guessing impractical. The probability of
   guessing one specific UUID in a single attempt is 1 in about 5.3 undecillion.

   This makes the UUID an opaque identifier, not an authorization mechanism. A
   leaked UUID can still be reused, so non-public resources require access-control
   checks as well.

9. Stop the local application. The runbook cleanup restores any fixture source
   files when it is executed through Sociable Weaver.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat target/application.pid)" 2>/dev/null || true
   rm -f 'target/application.pid'
   ```

### Internal and external identifiers

The numeric `id` remains the database primary key. It is compact, efficient for
local joins and indexes, and preserves the existing relational model. It is
predictable, however, so the application must not expose it as a public resource
identifier when enumeration is a concern.

The UUID is a separate, unique public identifier. It forms the boundary between
the API and the persistence model: controllers and external clients use the
UUID, while the data layer may continue to use the numeric primary key for
internal relationships.

UUIDs can also be used as database primary keys; that is a valid design with
different indexing, storage, and locality trade-offs. This example keeps the
numeric primary key to demonstrate that an API can stop exposing predictable
identifiers without redesigning every internal database relationship.

## Key takeaways and residual risk

- Sequential IDs made it cheap to discover and enumerate catalogue records.
- UUIDs make guessing identifiers impractical and reduce accidental exposure of
  predictable IDs.
- UUIDs are not authorization: a leaked UUID remains usable wherever the
  endpoint lacks an access-control decision.
- For non-public resources, explicitly authenticate the caller and enforce
  object-level authorization or tenant scoping on every request.
